messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel had moved to the United States from Southeast Asia as a child, and at 24 he lived with the quiet, guarded routines of someone who had learned to keep his head down. He worked as a painter, moving from house to house and job site to job site, carrying ladders, tarps, brushes, and cans of paint through unfamiliar buildings where he was expected to enter quickly, assess the space, and get on with the work. He was in a relationship now, but when he first came to treatment he described himself as already feeling apart from other people, as though he was living on the edge of things rather than inside them.

The relationship that became traumatic had begun as a source of closeness and then shifted into something he now described with visible hesitation. He did not go into every detail at first, but he was clear that the person he had been with physically hurt him. What stayed with him most was not a single dramatic moment but the experience of being trapped in the middle of it, trying to understand what was happening and when it would end. When he recalled that period, Daniel’s account became fragmented. Some parts came out in sharp, vivid detail — the room, the tone of voice, the sense of standing very still because any movement felt dangerous — while other pieces were blank. He would pause and say he could not remember the order of what happened, only that when he tried to think about it, it sometimes felt as if it were unfolding again in the present rather than being something finished in the past. At those times his body would tense and he looked less as if he were narrating a memory than enduring one.

In the months after the abuse, Daniel began noticing that certain moments would pull him back into it. An unwanted thought could arrive out of nowhere while he was working, and once it was there he would feel pulled into the same fear that had marked the relationship. He said he could not always control when these thoughts came, but when they did, they had a way of making the event feel near again. The same was true of uncertainty. If someone did not answer a message right away, or if a plan changed without explanation, he would find himself caught in the gap, imagining that something bad was happening and that he was missing it. Delays that others might brush off felt loaded to him, as though waiting itself could mean danger. He also noticed how strongly he reacted to the sense of being watched. In some settings — especially when he was alone in a room or moving through an unfamiliar building — he became acutely aware of other people’s eyes, as if he might be under observation without knowing it.

Over time, Daniel started structuring his days around those moments. At job sites he would scan exits as soon as he entered any room or house, noting which door was closest and where he would move if he needed to leave fast. He did this almost automatically, even before he had set down his tools. At home, he listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering the apartment, and he was especially alert when his evenings ran later than usual. If the day stretched out and night began to settle, he found himself increasingly on edge, waiting for nightmares he had learned to anticipate and avoid. He would try to keep himself busy or distract himself at those times, but he described this as a practical effort to stay ahead of the dreams rather than a way of feeling safer. He also avoided anything that reminded him of the man who had hurt him, including places, objects, and situations that carried even a hint of that person’s presence. He did not like saying more than that, but it was clear that these reminders had narrowed the places he felt able to go and the routines he could sustain.

When Daniel felt threatened, he sometimes froze completely. He described the reaction as frightening because it left him unable to do anything in the moment, even when part of him wanted to move away or speak. He had noticed this enough times to worry about how he might look to other people, especially at work, where he had to keep pace with others. The effort of staying alert and the cost of pulling back from reminders had started to show in the practical shape of his life. He found himself more restricted in where he went, more careful about how long he stayed in unfamiliar places, and more hesitant when plans were uncertain. Even in his relationship now, he carried a private fear that something about him made these things happen. He had come to believe that the abuse said something about the kind of person he was, that he was inadequate, and that he no longer belonged anywhere in the way other people did.

What brought Daniel to seek help was the growing sense that he could not keep managing these reactions alone. He was tired of watching every room for exits, tired of listening into the silence of his apartment for signs that someone was coming in, and tired of losing time to memories that arrived with the force of the present. He hoped treatment might help him feel less trapped by those moments, though what frightened him most was the possibility that he would always be living as if danger were just outside the door.
